newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Clinton hails N.Korean apology over submarine row.
newsitem.headline: Clinton hails N.Korean apology over submarine row.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton hailed North Korea's apology over a submarine incursion as a move towards peace, and South Korea on Monday agreed to return the bodies of intruders shot after landing from the vessel.
Handing over the remains of 24 intruders -- possibly on Monday -- would help clear remaining tensions from the infiltration of the North Korean submarine into Southern waters in September.
The bodies would be sent home via the border crossing point of Panmunjom on the fortified demilitarised zone that has split the two Koreas since the 1950-53 Korean War.
Out of 26 North Koreans set ashore from the submarine, 24 were shot dead -- 11 in an apparent mass suicide and the others by Southern troops. One was captured and one escaped.
Thirteen South Korean troops and civilians were killed during a massive manhunt.
In a belated apology on Sunday, North Korea expressed "deep regret" and mourned the "tragic loss of life". It promised such incidents would never recur and pledged to work for peace.

"I am pleased that Pyongyang has pledged to prevent the recurrence of such an incident and has expressed its willingness to work with others for durable peace and stability on the Peninsula," Clinton said in a written statement.
"I hope discussions can now begin to move forward on the four-party peace talks which President Kim Young-sam and I offered last April," Clinton said.
Clinton and President Kim invited North Korea and China to take part in talks aimed at securing a lasting peace to replace a truce that ended the Korean War.

The submarine incursion put on ice the peace initiative, froze international food aid to the hungry North and stalled implementation of a nuclear agreement under which Pyongyang pledged to halt its nuclear weapons programme.
South Korea's defence ministry said the bodies would be repatriated if North Korea made a request.

"Since North Korea has officially apologised and promised to prevent a recurrence of such incidents we have decided to return the bodies through appropriate channels if North Korea makes a request," a defence ministry statement said.
"We look forward to North Korea's cooperation towards peace and stability on the Korean peninsula."
A defence ministry official, who declined to be named, said South Korea would not return the captured agent or the submarine as Pyongyang has demanded.
Earlier, the United Nations Command said it may conduct a "repatriation of remains" ceremony as early as Monday.
The U.S.-led United Nations Command monitors a ceasefire that ended the Korean War and is the main channel of communication between the rival Koreas.
Pyongyang's apology was issued after U.S. and North Korean officials hammered out acceptable wording during intense negotiating sessions in New York.
Clinton thanked Kim for his efforts to resolve the issue "in a way that opens the door for future South-North dialogue".
Officials and diplomats in New York and Washington expected the apology to result in a series of steps to repair the damage to inter-Korean ties.

These could include a pledge from South Korea to resume construction work soon on two civilian nuclear reactors in the North and a simultaneous promise from North Korea to resume disposing of spent nuclear fuel rods.

Under a 1994 accord, North Korea agreed to give up its suspected atomic weapons programme in exchange for oil and a set of light-water reactors. But when Seoul put the project on hold after the submarine incursion, Pyongyang responded by halting work on overhauling its nuclear programme.
International food aid to North Korea could begin flowing again, U.S. officials said.
The U.N. World Food Programme planned to issue another appeal in the next few weeks. The United States may then pledge about $6 million in famine assistance.
